title: Buying The North Face in Nairobi: Which Pieces Earn Their Place on Kenyan Trails
meta_title: The North Face in Nairobi: 5 Ways to Buy Genuine Kit
meta_description: Where to find The North Face in Nairobi, which shells, fleeces and puffers suit Kenyan trails, how sizing runs and how to judge a thrifted piece.
excerpt: A practical guide to The North Face in Nairobi: the brand's key lines, which pieces suit Kenya's rains and Mt Kenya's cold, sizing, thrifted buying checks and where to find it.
content:
The most affordable way to own The North Face in Nairobi is second-hand. A pre-owned DryVent rain shell, a fleece in the Denali mould or a down puffer costs far less than new and still works on Kenyan mountains. Choose the layer your trail actually needs, check the fit and labels, and skip the pieces built for city streets.

The brand's logo is everywhere, which makes it hard to tell a mountain jacket from a fashion one, a tired thrift find from a good one, or a genuine item from a copy. Below we explain what The North Face is known for, which of its lines suit Kenya's rains and cold summits, how its sizing runs, how to judge a thrifted piece, and where to find The North Face in Nairobi without overpaying.

Quick Facts

  • Origin: The North Face began in San Francisco in 1966 as a small climbing and backpacking shop.
  • Logo: the three curved lines are a stylised Half Dome, the granite cliff in California's Yosemite Valley.
  • Waterproof fabrics: DryVent is the brand's own waterproof, breathable membrane; FUTURELIGHT is its more air-permeable premium version.
  • Best Kenyan uses: a shell for the short rains (October-December), a fleece for 2,000-3,000 m mornings, down for Mt Kenya's 4,985 m summit night.
  • Sizing: sizes are US-based, so compare the chest measurement in centimetres rather than trusting the letter on the tag.
  • Buying The North Face in Nairobi: thrifted stock of big brands changes week to week, so ask before you travel across town for one item.

What Is The North Face Known For?

The North Face is known for mountain shells, fleece and down jackets, tents and expedition packs. It grew from a San Francisco climbing shop into one of the best-known outdoor brands, and its top-tier Summit Series kit is still designed for high, cold mountains.

Two Bay Area climbers, Douglas Tompkins and his wife Susie, opened the first shop in 1966. Kenneth "Hap" Klopp took over soon after and moved the company into making its own gear. Since 2000 the brand has been owned by VF Corporation, the American group that also owns several other outdoor and clothing labels. You can read the brand's own account on The North Face's official story page.

Where do the name and logo come from?

In the northern hemisphere, the north face of a mountain gets the least sun, so it usually holds the most ice and is often the hardest side to climb. The founders took that as their name. The logo's three arcs trace Half Dome, a famous climbing wall in Yosemite National Park.

Which North Face lines matter for hikers?

The brand sells a huge range, from school backpacks to Everest suits. For hiking in Kenya, a handful of names cover almost everything you will see when shopping for The North Face in Nairobi:

  • DryVent: the house waterproof-breathable fabric, used in most of the brand's rain jackets and many insulated ones. Older jackets may say HyVent, its earlier name.
  • FUTURELIGHT: launched in 2019, a waterproof membrane spun from nano-scale fibres so that more air passes through. It shows up on higher-priced shells and Summit Series kit.
  • Nuptse: the boxy, baffled down puffer first made in 1992, with 700-fill down in the classic version. Warm, but bulky in a daypack.
  • Denali: a heavyweight fleece jacket from the late 1980s, with nylon overlays on the shoulders and chest. A favourite on second-hand rails.
  • ThermoBall: synthetic insulation shaped into small clusters that mimic down but keep more warmth when damp.
  • Summit Series: the technical line built for alpine climbing and expeditions.

The brand explains each of its fabrics on its technology page. Once you can read a label, sorting The North Face in Nairobi into hill kit and high-street kit gets much easier.

Which North Face Pieces Suit Kenyan Trails?

A waterproof shell, a mid-weight fleece and one insulated jacket cover nearly every Kenyan hike. Nairobi sits at about 1,795 m, most day hikes stay between 2,000 m and 3,000 m, and only Mt Kenya and the Aberdare summits push you into real cold.

The table below matches the common pieces of The North Face in Nairobi to the hikes where they earn their keep.

Rain shells for the short rains

A rain shell matters most from October to December and again from March to May. On the Ngong ridge or the Aberdare moorland, storms can roll in within an hour. Look for taped seams, a hood with a stiffened peak, and pit zips if you sweat on climbs. A 2.5-layer DryVent jacket is light and fine for day hikes; a 3-layer shell lasts longer under a heavy pack. Our post on choosing a rain jacket for Kenyan hikes explains the layer types in more detail.

Fleece for cold mornings

If you only buy one piece of The North Face in Nairobi, make it a fleece. A Glacier-weight quarter-zip handles a 6 a.m. start on Mt Longonot, while a heavier Denali suits camping or the drive up to the Aberdares. Fleece keeps some warmth when damp and dries in an hour of sun, which is why it works so well under a shell in rainy months.

Down and synthetic insulation for Mt Kenya

Before buying a down jacket from The North Face in Nairobi, be sure your trail goes high. Night temperatures at Shipton's or Austrian Hut regularly drop below freezing, and the climb to Point Lenana starts around 2-3 a.m. A dry 700-fill puffer is warm and compresses well. Down loses most of its warmth once soaked, though, so keep it in a dry bag and wear it under the shell in sleet. If your trip runs through rain, a ThermoBall jacket is the safer bet. Our guide to layering for cold weather hikes shows how these pieces stack together.

Packs and footwear

Many of the daypacks sold as The North Face in Nairobi were designed for commuting, so check for a hip belt, a chest strap and a bottle pocket before buying one for the trail. If you just need a hiking pack, our 28L day hiking backpack carries a shell, fleece and 2 litres of water comfortably. Hedgehog shoes grip well on firm paths, but Kenya's mud, ash and scree suit a mid-cut boot better.

How Does North Face Sizing Fit?

When you buy The North Face in Nairobi, remember that sizing follows US measurements. Many technical jackets run true to size, while lifestyle pieces such as the Nuptse are cut boxy and roomy. Always compare the chest measurement on the brand's size chart with your own, in centimetres, before you buy.

Product pages usually name the fit as slim, standard or relaxed. A standard-fit shell has room for a fleece underneath; a slim-fit one may only fit over a base layer. Women shopping for The North Face in Nairobi should note that women's pieces are cut narrower at the shoulders with more room at the hips.

Try this simple test when trying on The North Face in Nairobi in person: put on the fleece or puffer you plan to wear underneath, zip the shell over it, then raise both arms above your head. If the hem rises above your waist or the cuffs ride up your forearms, go up a size. Hood fit matters as well. With the hood up and cinched, you should be able to turn your head without the peak blocking your view.

Is Second-Hand The North Face in Nairobi Worth Buying?

Yes, second-hand The North Face in Nairobi is usually worth buying for mid-layers, insulation and packs, because the materials last for years. Waterproof shells need a closer look, since the seam tape and membrane age even when the outer fabric still looks good.

Quality thrifted gear is what lets many Kenyan hikers afford The North Face in Nairobi at all. A well-kept fleece from ten years ago keeps you as warm as a new one, and buying used keeps good kit in use for longer. Our post on thrifted outdoor gear in Nairobi covers the general rules for judging pre-owned kit.

What should you check on a thrifted North Face jacket?

Before paying for thrifted The North Face in Nairobi, run through these five checks yourself:

  1. Seam tape: turn the shell inside out and look along the shoulders and hood. Peeling or bubbling tape means the jacket will leak at the seams.
  2. Inner membrane: on a 2.5-layer jacket, a flaking or sticky inner coating means the waterproofing is finished.
  3. Zips and pullers: run every zip fully. A main zip that splits behind the slider is costly to replace.
  4. Down loft: squeeze a puffer and let go. It should spring back in a few seconds, with no flat, empty baffles or clumps.
  5. Fleece face: heavy pilling at the cuffs and underarms is cosmetic, but thin patches or holes at the elbows are not.

Small faults on second-hand The North Face in Nairobi often have easy fixes. A shell whose outer fabric soaks through but whose seams are intact often just needs washing and a fresh DWR (durable water repellent) treatment. A missing hood toggle or cord lock costs very little to replace.

How can you tell if a North Face item is genuine?

Counterfeit outdoor clothing exists everywhere, so anyone shopping for The North Face in Nairobi should know the general signs of a genuine item. None of these is proof on its own, and older or regional products can differ, so look at several together:

  • Logo embroidery: on genuine pieces the letters are clean and evenly spaced, with no loose threads joining them and the Half Dome lines sharply curved.
  • Labels: care labels are neatly printed, usually in several languages, and stitched in straight; misspellings and blurred print are warning signs.
  • Zips and hardware: zips run smoothly, often with branded pullers, and cord locks feel solid rather than flimsy.
  • Fabric and fill: a "700-fill" puffer that feels thin and flat, or a "waterproof" shell with no taped seams inside, does not match its label.
  • Price: a brand-new Summit Series shell at a fraction of its normal price deserves a second look.

If you are unsure about a piece of The North Face in Nairobi, compare it with photos of the same model on the brand's official website, paying attention to the logo position, zip layout and label style.

Pro Tips for Buying North Face Kit

  • Buy the layer you are missing, not the one with the most famous name. A cheap shell plus a good fleece beats a puffer with no rain cover.
  • Bring the mid-layer you already own when you try on a shell, so you size it for real use.
  • Read the inside label: "DryVent", "FUTURELIGHT" or "GORE-TEX" means waterproof; a plain nylon jacket is only wind- and shower-resistant.
  • If The North Face in Nairobi is out of stock in your size, a similar shell from another brand does the same job.
  • Pick bright colours for the Aberdares and Mt Kenya. They are easier to spot in mist.
  • Ask for the item by model name (Denali, Nuptse, Venture, Resolve) when you WhatsApp, as it speeds up the search.

How Do You Care for North Face Gear in Kenya's Dust and Rain?

Wash shells and fleeces gently, dry them fully and store them loose. Owners of The North Face in Nairobi face two enemies: dust and sweat that clog membranes, and damp storage that ruins down and loosens seam tape.

Wash a DryVent or FUTURELIGHT shell with a technical cleaner or a little mild liquid soap on a cool, gentle cycle, or by hand in a basin. Skip fabric softener, which coats the membrane. Rinse well, hang it in the shade and, once water stops beading on the surface, apply a spray-on DWR treatment.

Down needs more patience, and it is the priciest category of The North Face in Nairobi to replace. Wash a puffer only when it is visibly dirty, with a down-specific wash, then dry it slowly in the shade over a day or two, shaking the clumps apart every few hours. Store it loosely on a hanger rather than squashed in its stuff sack. Fleece is the easy one: wash it inside out to reduce pilling and dry it in the shade, because hard equatorial sun slowly fades and weakens synthetic fabrics.

Three Kenyan Hikes, Three North Face Kits

A worked example makes it easier to see how The North Face in Nairobi fits real trips. These three kits run from a half-day ridge walk to a summit night, adding one layer at each step.

Ngong Hills on a short-rains Saturday

On a 12-15 km ridge walk at around 2,400 m, you need little warmth but good rain cover. Wear a quick-dry T-shirt, pack a thin fleece and a light DryVent shell, the piece of The North Face in Nairobi you will use on almost every hike, and carry 2 litres of water. The shell goes on when the afternoon clouds build over the ridge.

Table Mountain in the Aberdares

The Table Mountain hike climbs to about 3,800 m through forest and bog, where wind and drizzle are common at any time of year. Add a Denali or Glacier fleece, a warm hat, gloves and waterproof trousers. A ThermoBall jacket in the pack covers long breaks at the top.

Mt Kenya to Point Lenana

For a 4-5 day trek to 4,985 m, you need the full system, whether from The North Face in Nairobi or other brands: thermal base layers, a fleece, a down or synthetic puffer, a 3-layer shell, insulated gloves and a balaclava. Our Mt Kenya gear shopping list and the wider hiking gear checklist for Kenya fill in everything else, from sleeping bag ratings to headlamps. Kenya Wildlife Service manages Mt Kenya National Park, so confirm current park fees and rules with KWS before you book.

Whichever kit you build from The North Face in Nairobi, one rule holds across all three: the heavier your insulation, the more it depends on a working shell above it. Spend your effort first on a shell that keeps the rain out, then build warmth underneath it.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is The North Face good for hiking or just for fashion?

The North Face makes both. Its DryVent and FUTURELIGHT shells, Summit Series kit, technical fleeces and trekking packs are built for real mountain use, while pieces like the 1996 Retro Nuptse are sold mainly as streetwear. Check the label for a waterproof fabric name and look for hiking features such as taped seams, a helmet-compatible hood or a hip belt before buying The North Face in Nairobi for the trail.

Which North Face jacket is best for Mt Kenya?

No single North Face jacket is best for Mt Kenya; a system works better. Pair a waterproof 3-layer shell with a mid-weight fleece and a down or ThermoBall puffer for the summit night, when the climb to Point Lenana at 4,985 m starts below freezing. Keep the down jacket in a dry bag during the wet forest and moorland days.

Are North Face jackets waterproof?

Only some pieces of The North Face in Nairobi are waterproof. Look for DryVent, FUTURELIGHT or GORE-TEX on the label, and check for taped seams inside. Fleeces, softshells, most down puffers and light wind jackets are water-resistant at best, so they need a shell on top during Kenya's long rains from March to May and the short rains from October to December.

Does The North Face run small or big?

The North Face uses US sizing, and most technical jackets run close to true size. Fashion-led pieces such as the Nuptse are cut wide and boxy, so some people size down. The safest method is to measure your chest in centimetres, compare it with the brand's size chart and try the jacket on over the layer you plan to wear underneath.

Final Thoughts

A logo on the chest does nothing at 5 a.m. on Point Lenana; the fabric, fit and layering do. Think of The North Face in Nairobi as a source of solid layers rather than a status label: a sealed shell for the rains, a fleece for cold starts and insulation only if your trail goes high.
